title: Pizzelle (Italian Waffle Cookies)
summary: Thin, patterned Italian waffle cookies pressed in an iron, crisp and light with a hint of vanilla and lemon, dusted with icing sugar to finish.
equipment: bowl and whisk or stand mixer or electric hand whisk

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt, or table salt

steps.title: Beat eggs and sugar
steps.text: Beat the eggs and caster sugar together for 3 minutes, until thick and pale. This builds air into the mixture, giving the finished biscuits a lighter, more delicate texture.

steps.title: Add butter and flavour
steps.text: Beat in the melted butter, vanilla extract and lemon zest until smooth. Adding the butter once melted and cooled stops it curdling the eggs.

steps.title: Fold in the dry ingredients
steps.text: Fold in the flour, baking powder and salt to make a thick, smooth batter that holds its shape briefly on a spoon; add 1-2 tablespoons more flour if it looks runny. A batter that's too thin will spread past the edges of the iron's pattern.

steps.title: Heat the iron
steps.text: Heat the pizzelle iron according to its instructions, which usually takes 5-10 minutes, and brush it lightly with oil before the very first batch only. After that, the butter already in the batter is enough to stop the cookies sticking.

steps.title: Cook each batch
steps.text: Drop a heaped tablespoon of batter just behind the centre of each pattern, close the iron and cook for 30-60 seconds, though timing varies between irons. Look for an even pale golden colour and for the steam from the iron to stop, which signals the cookies are cooked through.

steps.title: Shape while warm
steps.text: Lift the pizzelle onto a wire rack; they stay soft and pliable for a few seconds before crisping as they cool, so this is your window to roll them round a handle into tubes if you'd like that shape. Once crisp, they hold their shape permanently.

steps.title: Trim and finish
steps.text: Trim any ragged edges with scissors once the pizzelle are cool, then dust with icing sugar. Trimming after cooling avoids cracking the brittle biscuits.

tips: Watch the steam coming off the iron rather than relying only on the timer, as it's a more reliable sign that the pizzelle are properly cooked.
Shape or roll the pizzelle within seconds of lifting them out - a common mistake is waiting too long, by which point they've already crisped and will crack instead of curving.
Only oil the iron for the very first batch; oiling every time can make the cookies greasy and uneven in colour.
Keep the batter thick enough to hold briefly on a spoon, as a runny batter spreads beyond the iron's pattern and makes ragged edges.
Work in a calm, unhurried rhythm between batches, since the iron's temperature affects how evenly the next batch cooks.
Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week; keep them away from humidity, which softens their crispness. They can be frozen, unfilled and undusted, for up to 1 month.
